content: A persistent lymphocyte count of 8 x 10^9/L for more than six months has been observed, but the role of lymphopenia in cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) remains uncertain. Therapy should not be restarted if anaphylaxis or angioedema occurs. Clinically significant cases of liver injury have been reported, with onset ranging from a few days to several months after initiating treatment. Elevated hepatic transaminases, typically not exceeding three times the upper limit of normal (ULN), were observed during controlled trials and resolved upon discontinuation of treatment. If clinically significant signs or symptoms of liver injury occur, the drug should be discontinued. Serum aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and total bilirubin levels should be obtained prior to treatment and monitored during treatment as clinically indicated. Treatment should be discontinued if drug-induced liver injury is suspected. Available data from pregnancy registries, observational studies, and pharmacovigilance regarding the use of dimethyl fumarate in pregnant women have not indicated an increased risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. There is no data on the presence of dimethyl fumarate (DMF) or its active metabolite monomethyl fumarate (MMF) in human breast milk, nor on its effects on breastfed infants or milk production. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Dimethyl fumarate is generally considered acceptable during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. The drug is rapidly metabolized by presystemic hydrolysis via esterases in the gastrointestinal tract, blood, and tissues before reaching systemic circulation, where it is converted to its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF). Further metabolism of MMF occurs through the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, without involvement of the CYP450 enzyme system. Metabolites include MMF, fumaric acid, citric acid, and glucose. Excretion occurs primarily through exhalation of carbon dioxide (60%), with smaller amounts excreted renally (16%) and in feces (1%). Capsules should be swallowed whole and intact; they should not be chewed, crushed, or sprinkled on food. The medication may be taken with or without food, although administration with food may reduce the incidence of flushing by approximately 25%. Alternatively, taking non-enteric-coated aspirin (up to 325 mg) 30 minutes before each dose may reduce the incidence or severity of flushing. Capsules should be stored at 15–30°C (59–86°F), protected from light, and kept in their original container. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only.
